## Yama `ptrace_scope=3`, explained plainly

### The words, defined first

- **ptrace** = the Linux mechanism one process uses to watch and control another process, step by step. A debugger uses it. The Agent Firewall uses it: its monitor *traces* every program you launch with `run`, so it can pause each one at the moment it tries to do something dangerous.
- **Yama** = a security policy inside the Linux kernel. Its only job here: decide **who is allowed to ptrace whom**.
- **`/proc/sys/kernel/yama/ptrace_scope`** = a kernel setting (a number: 0, 1, 2, or 3) that says how strict that decision is.
- **TRACEME** = the call a newborn program makes to say "my parent may trace me." The firewall's launcher does this before the first program runs. If TRACEME is denied, the firewall cannot work at all.

### The four values

| Value | Meaning | Can the firewall run? |
|---|---|---|
| 0 | Any process of the same user may trace any other. Classic Linux behavior. | Yes. This machine had **0** for the whole project. |
| 1 | A process may trace only its own children. | Yes. Tracing your own children is exactly what the firewall does. GitHub CI runners use 1. |
| 2 | Only administrators (`CAP_SYS_PTRACE`) may trace anything. TRACEME is denied too. | No. |
| 3 | Nobody may trace anything. No exceptions. | No. |

### The rule that bit us

**Within one boot, the number can go up but never down.** Once the kernel has read a value, writing a smaller one fails with `EINVAL` — for root, for sudo, for everyone. This is intentional: it exists so that an attacker who gains control mid-session cannot *loosen* tracing restrictions. The only way back down is a **reboot**, after which the kernel reloads the configured default (on this machine: 0).

The agent doing the [af-12] hostile-same-UID measurements needed data for **all four values**. It raised the setting step by step with sudo: 0 → 1 → 2 → 3. At 3, the measurement was complete — and the door closed behind it. It tried to restore 0. The ...[truncated 1695 chars]

Mostly no — and the "yes" part is narrow and now measured. Let me be precise.

### First, correct one inference

Your machine is at 3 **because our measurement put it there** (with sudo, on purpose, to fill the yama 0–3 matrix). Scope 3 does not appear by itself. On a normal machine, nobody at 3 = nobody ever set it. The realistic values are below.

### The four values, and who actually runs them

| Value | Who runs this | Firewall runs? |
|---|---|---|
| 0 | Fedora's default; this machine's configured state | Yes |
| 1 | The **upstream kernel default**; Ubuntu, Debian, Arch, and every CI runner we used (GitHub, and Blacksmith's image) | Yes |
| 2 | Only machines hardened on purpose: CIS/STIG-style baselines, some server fleets | No |
| 3 | Only machines locked down even harder, on purpose | No |

So the default everywhere mainstream is 0 or 1, and **1 was designed exactly to permit what the firewall does**: a parent tracing the children it launched itself. The firewall does not attach to strangers; it is the parent of everything it watches. Scope 1 blocks gdb attaching to your already-running editor — it does not block a wrapper around a program it spawned.

### The real blocker class, stated exactly

- A machine at **2 or 3** is a machine whose administrator has said: *no process may trace another process, no exceptions.* A ptrace-based supervisor is incompatible with that policy **by the policy's own definition** — that is not a defect in the firewall, it is the setting working.
- Two facts make this narrower than it sounds: those values are rare, and they also forbid gdb, strace, and every debugger on that machine. A fleet that chose them has already decided it wants no tracing tools at all.
- The setting is **global per host** — not per container, not per user. A container on a scope-3 host is also blocked.

### Why a small VM is exactly the right answer

- **A VM has its own kernel.** Yama's dial belongs to the kernel, not the hardware. Inside a VM, the measurement agent can turn the dial 0 → 1 → 2 → 3, measure everything, and then you simply **throw the VM away**. The host never sees any of it. A VM reboot takes seconds; a host reboot takes your whole machine down.
- This is not a new trick — it is precisely why the CI runners kept working while this host was stuck: each CI job *is* a small throwaway machine. The VM lab just brings that same property local, with no queue and no minutes billed.

### One important boundary: VM yes, container no

Podman/Docker/toolbox are **not** a substitute here. A container shares the host's kernel, and Yama's setting lives in the kernel — so a container on this host is exactly as blocked as the host itself. (Podman *VMs* would work; podman *containers* would not.) If the test changes something kernel-global, it needs its own kernel.
